new_value:
Resolved as the bead itself recommended -- 'worth a comment so future contributors do not optimise it into something worse' -- plus a real asymmetry found while looking.

The comment: neither client sizes its buffer from Content-Length, and both now say why. A responder can promise the cap, send a hundred bytes, and make every fetch allocate the full limit; the header is untrusted and must not size an allocation. What the conservative 8 KiB start costs is Vec doubling, ~7 reallocations for a 1 MiB CRL, which is noise beside the network round trip and the 0.4-34 ms signature verification measured for PKIX-cr8.1. Raising the floor instead would penalise the high-frequency case, since an OCSP response is a few hundred bytes and 8 KiB covers it outright. So the existing value is well chosen and is now documented as deliberate.

The asymmetry: ureq had no Content-Length early-reject while reqwest did. Both enforced the same cap by different means, which is the divergence class worth closing. ureq now refuses before reading when the server has already promised more than the cap.

Test coverage consequence, which mattered: adding the early-reject made the existing 256-byte-body / 100-byte-cap test pass through the new path, leaving the read-time take(limit+1) enforcement uncovered. A chunked-response case now covers it (no Content-Length, so the early-reject cannot fire). Verified that removing the read-time check fails exactly that one test. Commit a829edc8.
